SUBJECT: Vanilla Quality Assurance Training Report- Managalas Afore LLG
Enclose is the full report for one week ( 22nd -26th October2018 ) Vanilla Quality
Assurance training funded by Melanesian with Partners and supported by local
Non-Governmental Organization - Managalas Conservation Foundation at Afore
Station, Afore LLG, Ijivitari District, Oro Province.
For your Information
Mark Gozapao
Principal Trainer

 1. Introduction
Highlands Vanilla Project was engaged & Funded by Partners with Melanesian (PwM), a well
renowned NGO based in Port Moresby to conduct week long Vanilla Quality Assurance
training at Managalas Conservation area, Afore LLG, Ijivitari District Oro Province.
The training was conducted for a week at Afore government station and attended by 57
vanilla growers/farmers and all highly appreciated the training and applauded sponsorPwM. It gives high opportunity & hope to produce quality pods to meet exportable
standard.
2. Vanilla History & its Economic power
How first vanilla was identified in Northern America in the 1700 and its market impact
on the lives of people growing vanilla in the world and in Papua New Guinea. All farmers
were shake up & sitting on their toes when we sum up this topic.
” Its totally interesting to cultivate a cash crop that can fetched very high value for our
communities were all government service is lacking here” said Lusian Loibambe, the
chairman of the Managalas vanilla Association.
3. Training
The training started on 22nd - 26th October 2018 at Afore station. The topics covered over
the week are;

2. Site selection- This topic covers the importance to avoid wrong

3. Planting of vanilla- Direct planting & Nursery planting
4. Mulching – How to make quick & effective nutrient for the vanilla
plant.
5. Field Management –

a. Weed control & Mulching

b.

Looping & tipping methods
c. Pollination

6. Flower induce- Technic to force vanilla produce flowerings at early

7. Pruning – Flower pruning, bean pruning & shade pruning and covers

8. Harvesting pod- how to identified that the pods are rip/ready .

 4. Field visitation
The farmers were taken into one participants vanilla plot near the station and show
them all farm management techniques. This part of the training is to get the farmers see
the actual demonstration of farm management tips, such as Mulching, Tipping, flower
pollination and they can effectively applied to their vanilla. In this session most farmers
asked a lot of questions and answered.

5. Quality Assurance Training
This part of the training leads up from harvesting of quality pods under the new training
skills imparted. More emphasis here to inform farmers that quality starts from garden.
What was given to the roots of the vanilla give the same result on the vine to beans.
a. Preparation before actual killing process
b. Water Killing process method & Sun killing method
c. Sun /outdoor drying
d. Indoor drying
e. Sorting process

 f. Market- Sell cured pods out locally & Internationally
6. Killing Demonstration
This process is to put stop to its growing hormones that are still active after harvesting from
vines.

7. Trained Farmers Respond/ Attendance
There were total of (57) fifty seven participants including three (3) female of which (54) fifty
four are male participant attended the training schedule for only 30 participants. The
coordinators of the training allow them to sit in and share the training materials. They were
very fortunate to attend this training and praised the PwM for the effort it made to make the
training possible.
8. Observation / Comments
Managalas area is estimated to be situated 600 meters above sea level (masl) that the
environment is conducive for vanilla cultivation and has already proven by giving high yields.
This also indicates that it can give high percentage of vanillin. The general government service is
lacking however people can make it happen. They can bring in tenderable development by

 increasing cash-flow at their rural station. Currently coffee buyers from Goroka were flooded in
Managals area buying coffee and others buying betul nut (buai). The farmers make comments
about building vanilla curing & processing mini house at ITOKAMA village, at the central
location.
9. Recommendation
a. The local vanilla farmers had struggled to plant vanilla with less information
however it produce positive result and had the actual plant growing vigorously
with high yield producing quality pod thus given an clear indication that the area
has a conducive climate. It is recommended that additional training must be
considered.
b. The follow up program for this particular training is schedule for another three
months’ time which is in the month of February 2019.
c. A mini Vanilla Curing & Processing station/house is highly recommended so that
all trained farmers and others can use the facilities during early stage to cure
their beans.
d. The local MP for the area may use this information and can excess training for its
communities.
e. Partners with Melanesian (PwM) will communicate with local representative to
give updated information on vanilla to Highlands Vanilla Project (HVP) for future
securing of Markets, Market for vanilla is highly guarantee. HVP has export
license & has steady international market.

10. Conclusion
In conclusion, Highlands Vanilla Project is a very experience NGO operating for over 18 years in
PNG with Christian principal to disseminate information to locals on vanilla cultivation & Quality
Assurance process. This water killing method is an international recognized and many farmers
in Northern Armerica, Costa Rica and even Madacasgar applied to produce high quality. We
have share our experience to the farmers and it is their responsibility to make it happen. We
can be contacted on our eail & mobile line for future discussion.

INTRODUCTION
The Script Writing Workshop under Theatre Training eventuated from the 23rd to the 30th of August
2018 with in the Managalas Plateau at Afore Station, Oro Province.
Before we went to Afore, we attended the last day of the Planning and MCF Board Meeting at Oro
Guest House which was attended by MCF Board, CBOs, PWM Board, Management and staff. The
purpose of the MCF Board meeting was to sort out outstanding issues and the Planning Meeting
was for the MOU signing between MCF and PWM Boards.

On Friday, the 24th of August we (Covey Wara Program Support Officer, Patrick Vuet Biodiversity
Coordinator and Hobert Poria Sustainable Livelihood Coordinator and myself) left Popondetta
Town at 1pm for Afore, it took us 5 to 6 hours by road to arrive at Afore Station.

 The other Program Coordinators went to Afore to carry out their individual and specific activities,
therefore we went as a group.
The Script Writing Workshop was conducted on Monday 27th to Wednesday the 29th of August in
which the Managalas Kuafeanami Theatre Group, MCF CBOs, Activity Coordinators and PWM
staff attended.

During the first day of the workshop, we had introduction of participants and identification of issues
which was raised from the Combine Forum last year and brought forward. We recapped on the
issues and highlighted nine (9) key issues which will be put into play segments and dramatized for
two weeks by MKTG during the Theatre Rehearsal which will be held in the East and West side of
the Plateau.
The next phase as agreed by participants during the workshop was ‘Community Empowerment’
through effective awareness. Also it was made clear during the workshop that one of the key issues
or the main focus of Managalas after the CA Declaration will now be on Sustainable Livelihood
Alternatives or activities.
On day two of the workshop, we (participants) went into groups and discussed on the main issues
we identified especially SLA and developed trigger questions.

./2

 Also, Patrick Vuet did an introduction into the establishment of the CA Committee, how they will
select their representatives and the guidelines to select representatives which were decided by locals
themselves.

./3

 Because of time constraints we skipped Learning Objectives and went straight into Trigger
Questions, also it was because issues to discuss were already identified during the Combine Forum
last year.
We divided ourselves into three groups and answered these questions;
 What is the role and responsibility of MCF with in the CA under SLA?
 What is the role and responsibility of PWM with in the CA under SLA?
 What is the role and responsibility of CBOs/LOs with in the CA under SLA?
From the answers gathered the MKTG got together and came up with play segments for rehearsal.
On the third day, we recapped and the MKTG did a mock theatre performance based on the
segments they came up with using the questions above.
Below is a brief description of the Script Writing Process;
a. Identify Issues
b. Write Stories
c. Come up with Learning Objectives
d. Identify Trigger Questions
e. Create Play Segments
f. Rehearsal
Below is a basic format of the Script Writing Process;

Note that, Theatre Performance by MKTG will be conducted for two weeks in the plateau before
the Zone Forum.
Finally, we achieved a lot during the Script Writing Workshop under the Theatre Training. We not
only concentrated on Script Writing and Theatre Training but also on other activities.
1. An introduction was made into the establishment of the CA Committee.
2. A basic run down of the Cash Trail was given to Alking (MKTG Director)
3. Crispine Burawa was understudying Alking to carry out the process of Script Writing.
PURPOSE
The main purpose of the workshop was to educate people by doing awareness, not just any
awareness but ‘education through performance.’ It is a process in which decisions are made in line
with what people want.
The next phase now in which MKTG will be focused on is ‘empowering the communities’ through
their performances surrounding the issues that were identified.
DISCUSSION
As discussed above, the key issues identified were;
./4

 1. Roles and responsibilities of MCF/PWM
2. SLA work in the plateau
3. Afore Council of Women
4. East CBO’s Petition
5. Establish Council of Chiefs for Advisory Body and LLG to pass law
6. Youth Program in the Plateau
7. Literacy Awareness in the 5 dialects
8. MoU for CA Committee Appointment
9. Establishment of Steering Committee
After the issues were identified, the participants went into groups and selected the most pressing
issues or the ones that needed to be addressed urgently which will now be the focus.
Thirty one participants that included ‘observers’ attended the Script Writing Workshop under
Theatre Training. There were many young men and women showed interest and joined the MKTG
last year. The MKTG has 12 full time members under its wings dedicated in creating awareness and
educating people through theatre.

There were 3 separate groups who attended the work shop, the MKTG, MCF and CBO Activity
Coordinators.
The main problem we faced was the involvement of CBOs during the workshop. The Script Writing
Workshop under Theatre Training was targeted at MKTG members and also CBOs, CBO Activity
Coordinators and CBO Managers. However, the attendance of CBOs was very poor, only Zone 5, 6
and 7B attended the workshop. The main reason being allowances not paid timely and other issues
of concern to them.
Because of the time factor, we skipped a process (learning objectives) and went straight into
developing trigger questions which will be put into play segments.
./5

 A major achievement recognized was the involvement of more young women in the theatre group.
There has been an increase in the number of women joining MKTG that shows that women are now
more aware and not afraid of reaching out to others, and educating them, through theatre regarding
the issues they face.
The workshop was successful because we exceeded the number of participants we anticipated. Even
though the number of CBOs there dropped, we had a good number of observers and women
representatives.
During the trip other PWM Program Coordinators also conducted their respective activities under
their programs in Afore and surrounding villages.
Overall, the trip was successful, we did encounter challenges however, the activity was carried out
smoothly.

RESULTS/FINDINGS
From the workshop, we identified the issues, discussed the different paths to take, organized and
assigned activities to respective participants who attended.
The next phase, which MKTG is going to take now, is to do rehearsals and performances within the
Managalas Plateau. They will be dramatizing the nine issues identified to create awareness and
educated the people in the East and West side of the plateau.
Also there are some issues which needs to be addressed or looked at;
 There needs to be a body that represent women in Afore. Therefore, during the work shop,
participants agreed that there should be more assistance towards the Afore Council of
Women, funding for its establishment, and there should be more representation. CBOs who
attended admitted that they failed in certain activities especially assisting women in wards
etc.
 More emphasis should be placed in assisting women form groups or associations in
accessing funding etc.
 Assistance into the urgent establishment of the CA Committee is needed.
 It was identified that there is a need for CBOs to have their own theatre group so that they
could do effective awareness within their own zones. MKTG will be the coordinating body
of all the 11 theatre groups.
 All agreed to focus more on the ‘next phase’, which is empowering the communities
through effective performances.

CONCLUSION
The Script Writing Workshop under Theatre Training was prosperous, in which pressing issues
were identified and laid out to be implemented through dramatization into the East and West side of
the Plateau.

./6

 Guidelines in selecting the CA Committee was also established which was decided by locals
themselves. Patrick Vuet gave an introduction into the establishment processes and requirements.
The workshop was successful because we exceeded the number of participants we anticipated.
During the trip other PWM Program Coordinators also conducted their respective activities under
their programs in Afore and surrounding villages.
The focus now has agreed by the workshop participants and is the way forward for Managalas after
the CA declaration is to put more emphasis on Sustainable Livelihood Alternatives.

Summary of Meetings with Arthur Ganubella at the Department of Environment and
Conservation
Jacinta Mimigari and Stephanie Safos
August 3, 2006
On our first visit to the DEC we were seeking more information about Management
Plans, as we had been examining the Management Plan draft that was completed by Philippa
Holden in 2003 and did not fully understand the function, purpose, and layout of the draft.
We were hoping that the DEC might have other examples of Management Plans or templates
that we could refer to in creating a Management Plan for the MCASP.
One particular area of confusion came up when it seemed as though large sections of
the Management Plan needed to be composed only after a Conservation Area was declared,
yet we were trying to write a plan that would be included in the application for a CA. When
we brought this up at the DEC, we discovered that the Management Plan is not supposed to
be included with the application at all but written only after the CA is declared. At this point
we were introduced to Arthur Ganubella, who talked to us more about the sequence of steps
that are to be taken when applying for a CA. We did not pay much regard to the specific
sequence of steps he described, as we assumed that PWM would already be aware of what
needed to be done. At this time we also met a man named Toby Ross from the Tree
Kangaroo Conservation Program. This organization has been working hand in hand with the
DEC in declaring Papua New Guinea’s first CA.
It was only after this meeting and after discussing what has learned with Vince that
we realized that more research needed to be done on the Conservation Area Act, and the
sequence of steps. We obtained a copy of the act and scheduled another meeting with Arthur.
In our second meeting with Arthur we asked him to again describe in detail the exact
steps that needed to be taken to declare a CA, and what the application process entailed. This
meeting was tape-recorder, noted, and accompanied by documentation (attached).
As a result of the meetings and research that has been done, it has become clear to all
parties involved that PWM has been miseducated about the CA declaration process, and as a
result of that miseducation has wasted time and other resources.
We feel that immediate action is needed. Specifically, PWM needs to initiate the
application process (as detailed in the attached) and make contact with the DEC, including
the officer that is based in Popendetta. One thing that was reiterated during meetings at the
DEC is that, because the declaration of a CA is not yet a streamlined process, it will only be
accomplished if done in close contact with the DEC and Park Services.
Our clear understanding of these proceedings is vital, as we intend to have Managalas
Plateau declared a CA and as an organization move into new areas as has been discussed.
Cc: Vincent Manukaysi- Programme Manager
Rufus. Mahuru- NLRP Administrator

clean_text:
The butterfly cowboy
By James Holden
“Oro! Oro! Oro! Oro!” cry the women from the tiny village of Voivoro. My companions
and I exchange uneasy looks, uncertain of the protocol or even the friendliness of this
greeting. The women approach, continuing their unnerving chant. But when they get
within arm’s reach they become silent, offering soft handshakes and bowing their heads
slightly. The eleven of us form an impromptu reception line as the men of Voivoro now
welcome us with their own gentle hands. The final man to greet us stands out from the
rest of the villagers dressed in their ragbag hand-me-downs. He appears quintessentially
Western and middle-aged in a crisp, pale blue shirt, light grey slacks and black slip-on
shoes.
He shakes our hands firmly, looking us in the eyes. His jaw-line is round and strong and
slightly shiny from a recent shave. He has a bulging brow-line overarching wide-set eyes
and a short, broad nose. He beams at each of us benevolently, showing straight white
teeth.
This is Russell Hauro, washed, clean-shaven, dressed up and ready to go to town.
A dozen timber-framed huts with palm-woven walls and grass-thatched roofs – Voivoro
is a seemingly unremarkable village of around 40 people. The hamlet is about an hour’s
drive along rough dirt roads from Popondetta, the capital of the Northern Province of
Papua New Guinea.
It’s not a particularly difficult journey in a four-wheel-drive as long as you know where
you’re going. There are no signs and after a while the oil palm groves that march away
from the roadways in cathedralesque columns tend to meld into one. The final turnoff is a
narrow track nearly overwhelmed by head-high Sudan grass. Take a detour through the
settlement of Ondahari to avoid the log blocking the track, drop down into a gully, across
a rickety drive-of-faith bridge, up a short rise and you’re there. When you arrive expect to
be greeted by the ladies of Voivoro, who will call out ‘Oro! Oro! Oro!” to you –
“Welcome! Welcome! Welcome!”

 For a physically- and emotionally-draining eight days we have been immersed in PNG
culture, Australian wartime history and most of all sweat. Yesterday we were a couple of
hour’s drive west of here – we were at Kokoda Station drinking SP beer and telling
improbable stories about our adventure on the infamous track of the same name.
But today we have come to Voivoro to see Russell Hauro’s butterflies.
PNG village life is almost entirely dependent on local resources available, so Russell
Hauro – as village chief and head of the community council – decided to make use of
Voivoro’s greatest natural asset, Queen Alexandra’s birdwing, arguably the world’s rarest
butterfly. Unlike other species, which are seen throughout PNG, Queen Alexandra’s
birdwing is only found in three small populations, one of which is on the plains near
Popondetta. If that’s not enough to attract butterfly enthusiasts, it is also the world’s
biggest – adult females have wingspans up to 300 mm. That’s slightly larger than an
average-sized dinner plate.
What the male lacks in size he makes up for in colour. With his aqua-green and cobalt
blue markings, he is a queen in name and nature. His patterns radiate out from a fat
yellow, Cuban-cigar-abdomen in feathery brush strokes that contrast vividly with a black
background canvas. The female is big and drab brown with the odd splash of yellow.
Compared to Mr Mardi Gras the poor love looks like she needs a good spruce up.
Although he is officially retired, Dr Don Sands is still fired by butterfly passion. So he
comes into work at the CSIRO (Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research
Organisation) laboratories in Brisbane a couple of days a week, even though his salary
has long ceased.
Don is a stoutish, shortish man with a full head of grey hair and together we squeeze into
his three-metre square office. The cubicle is packed with a lifetime’s research – papers
and loose-bound documents cover most of the benches. As Don is telling me the recent
history of the Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly in PNG he frequently jumps up,
pulling down thick textbooks from overloaded shelves to prove a point or to show me
how to spell a taxonomic name. There is a faint smell of mothballs emanating from one

 corner. There, about half a dozen wooden boxes are stacked. They contain pinned
butterflies, caterpillars and chrysalises preserved with crystals of naphthalene.
In a measured tone that reminds me of Barry Humphries delivering a well-considered
monologue, Don tells me of a Belgian called Ray Straatman who, starting in the 1950s,
worked for the Australian government in PNG for two decades.
“Ray was a brilliant biologist,” Don says with evident admiration. “He discovered the life
cycles of many of the Papuan birdwings, including alexandrae,” he continues, using the
second part of the butterfly’s scientific name.
“He took on-board several Papua New Guinean young lads to collect butterflies for him.
“Ray was probably gay,” he says matter-of-factly “although we never really found out,”
he qualifies.
He adds that Ray was a partisan in the Second World War – his speciality was blowing
up German trains. After the war, Ray immigrated to Australia and joined CSIRO.
Don says Russell Hauro was one of Ray Straatman’s students. From Ray, the young
Russell learnt how to breed, catch, prepare and pin birdwing butterflies. But Russell
discovered the value of Queen Alexandra’s specimens for himself.
“In the early 1960s a large number of collectors were working out of PNG – many of
them Japanese – hiring locals to hunt birdwings.”
Collectors were offering Papuans between one and two hundred dollars for a pair in good
condition. These would be sold on as cased specimens for between two and five thousand
dollars, depending on the quality and size of the butterflies.
“The villagers were so good at spotting them, collecting started to threaten some of the
species – it just couldn’t continue.”

 So Australian laws, later superceded by PNG laws, were passed in 1968 that protected all
but two common birdwing butterfly species in PNG. It became illegal to farm, collect or
trade in birdwings without a permit. And permits were not issued for Queen Alexandra’s.
But illicit trade in the rare butterfly continued throughout the 1970s.
“Boxfuls of unset (unpinned) specimens were still being bought by Japenese collectors.
And we all know where most of them came from,” Don says with a conspiratorial grin.
In the 1980s the International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources
(IUCN) passed an international law, categorising many of the birdwings from PNG as
protected. Queen Alexandra’s was becoming so rare it was classed as endangered – all
international trade was strictly forbidden.
Some twenty years later in May 2000, Russell found himself taking the first plane
journey of his life courtesy of the Canadian government. At the Vancouver Provincial
Court, Gilles Deslisle, a French Canadian from Quebec, was being tried for importing
Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly specimens. Russell was the star witness for the
prosecution. He alleged that Deslisle acquired six specimens from PNG between 1996
and 1999. This was not second hand information or rumour – Russell was well
acquainted with the facts because he was the person who supplied Deslisle with the
butterflies. He received between $350 and $500 for each specimen – on the black market
they are worth up to $30,000.
Russell was portrayed as “an exceedingly unsophisticated individual” who was bribed by
the self-taught amateur entomologist Deslisle to collect the specimens. Russell did
nothing to dispel this bucolic image when he needed help to use hotel lifts.
Although the appeals court judge found Deslisle’s motives were “ego satisfaction, rather
than monetary gain”, she upheld the original decision to fine the Canadian $80,000.
After the initial court case, Russell returned to Voivoro, where he was given a hero’s
welcome. He was now a local celebrity – no one from the village had travelled out of the
Northern Province, let alone to another country.

 In January 2001 Russell was granted full immunity from prosecution for conspiring to
export an endangered species. The decision had been based on advice from lawyers
involved in the Canadian court case. It was as if Russell was seen as a victim rather than
a fellow perpetrator.
According to Dr Don Sands the incident, and the years of black-market trading in Queen
Alexandra’s that preceded it, would not have occurred if his suggested plan had been
implemented.
In 1996 the Australian Agency for International Development (AusAid) funded a study of
Queen Alexandra’s birdwing in PNG. The seven million dollar project was conducted by
AACM – a South Australian company specialising in natural resource management. The
principle researcher, Christopher Mercer, reviewed all the research, completed intensive
monitoring, and then suggested ways of conserving the butterfly.
Don Sands was the consultant entomologist for the four-year study.
Don does not criticise the project’s methodology. But he feels locals such as Russell –
although he took part in a vine-planting program to increase the density of the
caterpillar’s food source – should have been more involved.
“Russell knew lots of snippets of information that no one else was aware of – for instance
he knew that alexandrae chose some food-vine plants over others.”
He is also less than impressed with Mercer’s suggestions for conservation, which, he says
do little to encourage locals to look after the species.
Don says the critical thing about Queen Alexandra’s birdwing is its enormous size. The
larger the specimen, the more it is worth.
“In the wild you get a range of sizes. But I had developed, through my work with the
Richmond birdwing butterfly here in Australia, a method of making adults very big. It’s
related to nutrition in the caterpillar stage.”

 Don proposed – under government supervision and through a strictly controlled breeding
program – that a small number of Queen Alexandra’s should be released onto the world
market each year, effectively putting an end to black-market trade.
Only the largest and most valuable specimens would be sold, the rest would be released
into the wild, supplementing the natural population. The income from the sale of the
butterflies would be distributed to the villages on a proportional basis, depending on how
much they were doing to conserve Queen Alexandra’s birdwing.
“It was foolproof. CSIRO approved it; the project’s lawyer approved it, but AACM
didn’t want to know, so it fell flat,” Don says, clearly disappointed even four years after
his recommendation was rejected.
Russell was also disillusioned with the project’s outcomes.
Hoping to attract overseas visitors to the village, he built a guesthouse at the start of the
AusAid study. It was a bold move that he says cost him in excess of than $10,000 – more
than a lifetime’s earnings in Papua New Guinea. It even rated a mention in the 1998
edition of the Lonely Planet guide for PNG, which said, “(the ecotourism lodge) is a
chance to support the income-earning efforts of rural people.” But shortly after this
Lonely Planet withdrew their PNG guide from publication because of safety concerns for
tourists.
About the same time the AusAid project was finalised and the income Russell and the
villagers were getting for monitoring Queen Alexandra’s birdwing disappeared.
For two years Russell struggled on with his ecotourism lodge and butterfly sanctuary. But
the tiny trickle of visitors all but dried up.
Eventually Russell became so angry and frustrated he invited officials from the provincial
government, local conservation groups and the oil palm industry to Voivoro. Dr Paul
Nelson, an ex-pat Australian and the agricultural research manager for the Oil Palm
Research Association, was there.

 “When we arrived at the village, there was a woven-palm barricade blocking the
entrance,” Paul recalls.
He says as the group approached the wall they heard a voice call out.
“Are you the father and mother of the environment?” it challenged.
“No one knew what to say, so we just stood there in silence.”
The voice called out again, with more force, “Are you the father and mother of the
environment?” Silence again.
“It was getting embarrassing by this stage, but finally someone replied ‘Yes!’”
But Paul says the inquisition wasn’t over. “Have you come here to help or just to look?”
the voice demanded.
“Thankfully someone answered almost immediately this time, saying we were there to
help and the barricade was opened.”
There was Russell, ready to challenge his guests in ceremonial dress, including a
magnificent headpiece made from the resplendent feathers of the bird of paradise.
“He danced towards us and thrust a spear into the ground near our feet. Then he pulled it
out, retreated a few steps and stabbed the ground again.
“Finally he let us into the village, and we sat down and had a sing-sing and a feast as if
we were all best mates,” Paul remembers with a smile.
Russell had made his point. And nothing changed.
But Russell did have one small win. Ever the supreme opportunist, as the official party
left he asked them to take his lawnmower into Popondetta for repairs.

 Today Paul Nelson is back at Voivoro. He has brought us to visit Russell Hauro and
hopefully to see his butterflies. Russell tells Paul he wants to charge the group 20 kina
(about 10 dollars). This will include entry into the village for the group and a guided walk
through the rainforest that surrounds the village. At less than a dollar each, the price
seems extraordinarily cheap. But Russell plays his first opportunist card of the day – he
says if we want to take a photo of a Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly, each picture
will cost 50 kina, including those of a caterpillar or chrysalis.
When Paul conveys this information to the group a brief discussion ensues. We decide 25
dollars split eleven ways is a mere pittance for this photo opportunity. And we nominate
Ingrid, an athletic Australian of Danish extract, as our official photographer. This is
partly because she has the best camera – which she lugged in its heavy plastic case for the
length of the Kokoda Track – and partly because she seems to know how to use it. These
are pertinent points because the group has decided she is only going to get one shot at it.
Russell’s son David will be our guide. He is a quiet man in his early 20s of average
height and build for a Papuan, which is about 170 cm tall and nearly the same around the
chest. He leads the way out of the village along a well-used path. In single file we follow
his broad frame into a tunnel of dense undergrowth.
David is dressed ready for a visit to Popondetta with his father, except he is wearing his
purple and gold Bronco’s rugby league shirt inside out. David says he wants to keep it
clean. When he gets to town, he’ll turn it the right way round.
After a few minutes the path reaches a shallow river with sunlight dappling the gentlyflowing current. We wade through the stream, not bothering to remove our sandals.
As we climb the slippery bank on the other side, Greg Shannon, a typically laconic
Australian, turns to me and says, “I thought we’d finished with this shit.”
After another five minutes David pauses, perhaps for effect, and he looks up into the
canopy. He points out the climbing vine that is the staple diet of the birdwing’s caterpillar

 stage and grows thick and lush on the phosphorus-rich volcanic soils of the Popondetta
Plains.
Don Sands believes vine nutrition is what limits the butterfly to this area. And he says the
rapid growth of the oil palm industry has destroyed much of the butterfly’s habitat,
driving it towards extinction.
We all stop and look upwards hoping to see an iridescently-coloured dinner plate flutter
into view. David crosses the track and grabs a hand-sized leaf. He flips it over exposing
pale green varicose-like veins. The group gathers around.
A yellow and brown scaly lump is attached to the partly-chewed leaf by its spiny bottom
and a stiletto-thin spike.
We have found the Queen Alexandra’s birdwing butterfly. If we came back in a few days
we could watch this three-inch long pupa break open. If we were patient and watched for
three more days we could see it slowly unfold its ruler-wide wings. We could witness the
metamorphosis of what is perhaps the most rare, most spectacular, and undeniably the
largest butterfly on the planet.
As it is, we have to make do with a yellow and brown protuberance that sits motionless
on a vine leaf.
But the indefatigable Ingrid is not disheartened. She brings the camera up to her face and
prepares to record the event – or rather, the lack of one. But at the last minute she pauses,
then passes the camera to Paul, saying, “I think I’ll hold the leaf.”
In other words, “You’re the one responsible for us being here, you can be the one to
waste $25 on a picture of a lump on a leaf.” Fair call, I’d say.
Paul shrugs and takes the camera; Ingrid takes the leaf. One more helper is required – at
least their shoulder is required – to act as a human tripod. I can’t resist taking a photo of
the photographer and his assistants. David glances at me after my flash goes off – I hope

 I’m not going to be charged $25 for taking a photo of someone taking a photo of a lump
on leaf.
The irony is,” Paul says as he completes his shot, “Queen Alexandra’s are mostly seen in
people’s gardens.”
Greg gives me another laconic look and we head back to Voivoro.
But Russell is not finished with us. At the village he approaches Paul holding the money
he gave him when we arrived. Together they walk to the corner of the communal hut – a
palm-thatched pagoda with a raised floor.
“Here is your 20 kina,” Russell says showing the grubby note to Paul. “Now you owe 130
kina.”
When Paul questions this Russell says, “Yes, 20 kina to come to the village, 50 kina for
the photo and 80 kina to leave.”
Paul quickly realises the futility of arguing and hands Russell the outstanding money.
“By the way,” Paul says as we walk back to the vehicles, “we’re also giving Russell and
David a lift into Popondetta.”
Depending on the occasion Russell Hauro has several hats that he likes to wear – village
chief, local hero, businessman, conservationist and erstwhile star witness in a Canadian
court.
But his favourite is undoubtedly his town hat, which he is wearing now as he sits in the
backseat of Paul’s dual cab utility. It’s a black Stetson, which has emblazoned across the
brow in bold white letters – COWBOY.

Queen Alexandra’s Birdwing Butterfly
(Ornithoptera alexandrae Rothschild).

A review

W.W. Page, Senior Entomologist, Oil Palm Research Association,
PO Box 97, Kimbe, West New Britain Province 621,

 Papua New Guinea.

 Introduction
The Queen Alexandra’s Birdwing butterfly (Ornithoptera alexandrae, Rothschild) is, justifiably,
an insect that deserves a lot of attention both because of its size and its localised habitat, which
contributes to its perceived rarity. QABB, as it will be referred to throughout this review, is
recognised as the world’s largest butterfly with the female wingspan ranging up to 30cm and
male wingspan up to 24cm. Because of this, it came under a lot of pressure from collectors in the
early to mid parts of the last century and has been constantly under pressure from shifting and
permanent cultivation, logging, volcanic activity and changes in weather patterns. Much has
been said and written about QABB and, because of it’s high profile, many people from different
walks of life have become involved in one way or another (e.g. farmers, land owners, collectors,
traders, conservationists, scientists, donors and politicians). There has therefore been an
accumulation of facts, conjecture, informed and uninformed statements that have been passed
down over time. The purpose of this review is to examine what is known about QABB and to
bring together the various ideas on its conservation and to suggest a way forward which can be
adopted by the various stakeholders to ensure continuity in conservation for the future. The
review is based on various papers, reports, file notes and some interviews with officers who are
working or have worked on the study and conservation of QABB. Unfortunately the author has
not sighted some important reports, and has had to rely on other reports, reviews and papers to
glean the information contained in those reports.
Alfred Meek first collected QABB near or around Kokoda in January 1906 and it was named by
Lord Rothschild (Meek’s employer) in 1907 in honour of Queen Victoria’s sister, Alexandra.
Meek had to shoot the female specimen down with a shotgun as it was flying high in the canopy.
He did not specify the area very clearly other than he was at “Biagi, 5000ft high, at the head of
the Mambare River” The Biagi tribe were said to be on the upper slopes of the mountains
“plainly visible from Kokoda”. With a locality description like this it is difficult to know exactly
where the specimen was collected other than it was not at Kokoda itself. Mercer (1999) says that
the butterfly has never been recorded in the Kokoda area since, although Parsons (1992) reports
unconfirmed sightings in the area during the 1980’s. Meek also caught the first male specimen
about a year later (1907) and his locality for this specimen was even vaguer than for the first
female: a “position under the Owen Stanley ranges”, which has been presumed to be around
Popondetta. The two type specimens for this species therefore have very poorly recorded
locations. By the end of 1908 Meek had collected perfect specimens of both male and female
QABB and had also found the larvae and pupae.
Between the early collections and the 1960s, a general outline of the life cycle of QABB was
established. Along with most of the other birdwing butterfly species, QABB became highly
collectable and various collectors and dealers trained local people to collect and rear the larvae
and pupae so that perfect specimens of the butterflies could be obtained. This caused concern
amongst some entomologists who recognised that, because the localised nature of QABB’s
distribution, there was a danger of the species being over-collected and the butterfly becoming
extinct. Legislation was therefore brought in to protect seven species of birdwing butterflies
under the Fauna Protection Act (1968), which was superseded by the 1974 Fauna (Protection and
Control) Act. This act prohibits the killing, selling, buying or possession of a protected species.
The International Union of Conservation of Nature (IUCN) lists QABB as endangered. QABB is

 also said to be on Appendix 1 of the Convention on International Trade of Endangered Species
(CITES). Various authors (e.g. Mercer, Orsak, Douglas) state that QABB was put onto
Appendix 1 during the 1980’s, several authors sighting Collins and Morris 1985. However in
1992, Parsons, who originally suggested and campaigned that QABB should be on Appendix 1,
says: “This recommendation was later adopted in print by Collins and Morris (1985) but, to date,
O. alexandrae remains on Appendix II”. According to the CITES website QABB is on Appendix
1. Despite the legislation, many collectors and dealers have been caught with QABB and, given
the high price paid for an individual specimen in Europe and America (over $1000); the
temptations are high for illegal trading.
There have been a number of studies of the biology, ecology, distribution, habitat and
conservation of QABB and various strategies have been developed. The history of these studies
can be summed up as follows:
a. 1970-71. Ray Straatman was commissioned by the PNG Government to carry out the first
detailed study of QABB. He produced sketch maps of three areas near Popondetta where the
butterflies could be found, discovered a population between Afore and Sila, made initial
descriptions of the habitats and produced a study on the life cycle of QABB.
b. 1979-1996. Michael Parsons was at the Insect Farming and Trading in Bulolo between 1979
and 1983. During this time he made several visits to Oro Province to survey the distribution
of QABB and other butterflies and wrote a series of reports and papers between 1980 and
1984 (7 relevant to QABB). His four main reports to the PNG Division of Wildlife covered:
(i) continuation of Straatman’s work, giving new localities of QABB populations on
Popendetta plain (ii) oil palm development, concluding that it is incompatible with QABB
presence in same area (iii) the likely effects of logging on Popendetta plain by Kumusi
Timbers (iv) proposals for three conservation sites known to have large QABB populations:
Siai / Mangure, Girigirita / Ongoho, and Huhuru / New Warisota. Parsons also made periodic
visits to PNG during the rest of the 1980’s and produced a number of high profile reports and
papers between 1985 and 1990. In 1991 he carried out a two-month survey of QABB on the
Popondetta plain with a short visit to Afore/Kawowoki on the nearby Managalase Plateau.
He then produced a comprehensive review of the state of knowledge of QABB in 1992 and a
paper proposing revisions of the genus of Aristolochia (food vines of several of the
birdwings) in New Guinea and Australia. In 1998 he produced “The Butterflies of Papua
New Guinea: Their Systematics and Biology” a 928 page book covering 958 butterfly species
with photos of 3000 specimens and 400 colour photos detailing aspects of life history and
ecology. Michael Parsons is regarded as the world authority on QABB.
c. 1984. W. Moi produced reports to the Office of Environment and Conservation on habitat
conservation.
d. 1992. Larry Orsak produced, at the request of the PNG Department of Environment and
Conservation (DEC), a five-year management plan for QABB. This covered (i) a summary of
the existing knowledge of QABB, speculating the reasons why it is a rare insect (ii)
organisations participating in the conservation of QABB (iii) a framework for a conservation
programme (iv) strategies for success of a conservation programme (v) biological
considerations in the conservation of QABB (vi) a management action plan with key
outcomes
e. 1998. Simon Saulei carried out some limited work on QABB habitat.

 f. 1991-1994. DEC, Chris Mercer, and students from Unitech carried out a number of surveys
to delineate further the distribution of QABB. The surveys resulted in the known range of
QABB being increased by 50%, and suggested that Managalase Plateau has the main QABB
population.
g. 1995 – 1999. The Oro Conservation Project was instigated under a component of a World
Bank loan for the expansion of smallholder oil palm blocks in Oro Province. After
discussions, the QABB conservation component was transferred to a grant program under
AIDAB (now AusAid) auspices. The project pooled the resources of the AusAid Project,
DEC and the Oro Provincial Government in promoting research and conservation of QABB.
The project covered various areas of research on QABB: (i) distribution (ii) monitoring (iii)
habitat creation and enrichment planting (iv) captive rearing (v) biology and ecology (vi) food
plant ecology and taxonomy (vii) the effects of environmental disturbance and (viii)
conservation. Chris Mercer, the Principal Scientist on the project, wrote a final report in
1999.
h. Since the end of the above project there has been little work done on QABB. A workshop of
interested parties was held in 2001 to discuss future conservation needs but little transpired
from that. Also in 2001, John Douglas produced an assessment for DEC of further actions
needed to protect QABB. OPRA and HOP have been involved in carrying out monitoring
surveys, working on the propagation and planting out of the food vine for QABB and have
been helping the Government Offices (the Provincial Wildlife Officer and the DEC
representative for Oro Province) in encouraging and organising the setting up of Wildlife
Management Areas.

Life cycle
The whole life cycle
Total life cycle takes 9 ½ weeks, just less than five months
QABB activity is seasonal
Caterpillars are most frequently found during the wet season when the vines put on new leaves
Opposite for adult butterflies – seldom seen during the wet season, common from May to
October
Mortality factors include a hymenopteran parasitoid, possible nematode infections, spiders and
possibly birds

The imagos (adult butterflies)
Males are metallic- blue/green with a wing span of 22-24cm
Females are brown and orange/yellow with a wing span of 27-29cm
QABB from Managalase Plateau are much larger than those from Popendetta Plain
Adult QABB are strong fliers and cover long distances
Males and females have a courtship dance prior to mating
Both sexes visit a number of flowering trees, vines and bushes to obtain nectar
Trees include Kwila, Teak and Kleinhovia sp
Vines include Morning Glory and Tobatoba
Bushes include Hibiscus, purple Ipomea, Bougainvillea and Ixora, as well as coffee (during
flowering)

 The ovae
Egg stage – 12-14 days,
Egg deposited either on underside of leaf of food plant vine, or under leaf of the supporting tree

The larvae
6 larval instars – 72-75 days,
3-day pre-pupal stage
Males generally go through 5 instars and female 6
Those raised on highly nutritious vines often skip one of the later instars
First and second instar caterpillars can only chew tender new leaves
1st and 2nd instar caterpillars feed on new leaves and the growing tip of vines
As caterpillars get older they progressively move down the vine to feed on older and tougher
leaves

The pupae
pupal stage of 49 days
4 pupation sites
1. under a vine just below the tree canopy
2. under a leaf in crown of tree
3. under a vine leaf close to the last feeding site, usually within five metres of ground
4. pupate under a leaf in nearby bushes, up to 10 m away from vine

Distribution
Distribution on Managalase Plateau and surrounding coastal hills
Butterfly monitors set up at Kawowoki , Tabuane, Tahama and Toma
Have all found immature stages of QABB
Caterpillars also sighted at Koruwo, Siribu, Semehara and at intervening sites across plateau
Following villages found in areas of QABB habitat and recommended for conservation:- (1)
Semehara, (2) Toma, (3) Gewoia, (4) Korala, (5) Umbara, (6) Dareki, (7) Sigara, (8) Kawowoki,
(9) Afore, (10) Yoivi, (11) Yoivi, (12) Kweno, (13) Tabuane, (14) Dea, (15) Koruwo, (16)
Tahama, (17) Siribu
Distribution at Collingwood Bay
Lowland form of P. dielsiana foodplant widely distributed in Wanigela area of Collingwood Bay

 QABB not found in this area
Vines grow in abundance on nutrient rich soils derived from volcanic ash, in similar conditions as
in Popendetta Plain and Managalase Plateau
Cape Ward Hunt
2 QABB found at Taututu along Mambare River
Very few vines located and no immature stages of QABB sighted
Seems to be a very small, isolated population

Popendetta Plain
Mostly a mosaic of forest fragments interspersed with Imperata grassland
QABB habitat remains of the slopes of Mount Lamington and to the north and west of the Plain
Oro Conservation Project has focused its research and conservation efforts at three sites:(1) the proposed Voivoro Wildlife Management Area at Ondahari (approx 400 ha) in north-west
(2) the Hombareta Wildlife Management Area (approx 130 ha) in the centre
(3) the Gewota / Sananada proposed WMA (approx 800 ha) in north-east, near to coast
Enrichment planting with vines has been going on at Voivoro and Hombareta since early 1970
Voivoro is one of best sites for QABB
Hombareta does not appear to have QABB any more – is now completely surrounded by oil palm
130 ha Hombareta WMA appears to be too small to sustain a continuous QABB population
Appears to be a lower critical size to a reserve, below which the habitat can no longer sustain
QABB habitats
Effects of environmental disturbance on QABB habitat
shifting cultivation results in forest clearance
has intensified over past 20 years with increasing population
many areas in Managalase Plateau are running out of land, resulting in shortened rotation times
vegetation becomes degraded and QABB vines do not grow

Habitat
Pararistolochia dielsiana (??) vines have a far greater distribution than QABB, but QABB is
restricted to 3 areas in Oro Province
Thought to be the quality of the volcanic soils promote vigorously growing vines at high density
Chemical cues determine the initial stages of oviposition behaviour
Perhaps combined with a visual cue
Vine density said to be important factor in inducing oviposition:-

 100+ vines / ha – excellent habitat
50-100 vines / ha – good habitat
50-30 vines / ha – frequently utilised
10-30 vines / ha – occasionally utilised
less than 10 vines/ ha – seldom utilised
Forest structure also important in determining if vines are to be utilised, even with good vine
density
Primary and secondary forest sites utilised by QABB show openness
5 metre + gap between canopy trees and next tree storey

Interaction with the host plants
Larval food plant Pararistolochia dielsiana
Adult nectar food plants
Behaviour
Female QABB will not oviposit on a vine that already has an immature stage of either its own
species or Ornithoptera priamus already on it (Straatman and Parsons say the opposite: can get
many larvae on one vine but none on vines nearby)
Female QABB will only deposit one egg per vine
Growth phase of vine is important in inducing oviposition
Female will deposit egg within 2 metres of actively growing shoot
Vines with no growing shoots are usually not chosen as oviposition sites

Attempts at conservation
Legislation
Conservation areas
Oil palm results in the complete destruction of QABB habitat in areas where it is grown.
Impossible for vines to grow in oil palm agroecosystem (??)
Proposed that reserve areas of forest should be left throughout HOPPL estates
One such reserve was 100 ha forest at Lejo Forestry Station
This area was mostly planted with oil palm by 1995
Before VOP blocks are established in forest areas inspections should be made to determine if
areas are significant QABB habitats
Areas with good vine density should be preserved
Commercial logging commenced on the Popendetta Plain in early 1980s
No commercial logging yet on the Managalase Plateau or surrounding coastal hills

 1986 Oro province Forestry Plan considers most of the province for logging
Logging opens up previously inaccessible areas, resulting in QABB habitat fragmentation and
reduction
Strict adherence to the Logging Code of Practice including a 40 year regeneration period and the
provision of an adequate system of reserves is necessary if QABB populations are to be sustained

Captive breeding
Captive breeding studies
Flight cage and shade house fabricated in Lae and erected at Afore
Both semi-circular in profile
Flight cage is 20m long, 4m wide and 3.5m high, covered with 2 x 40% white shade cloth
Shade house only 7.5m long, covered with 40% green shade cloth
Shade house used to study feeding behaviour of QABB, to determine life cycle lengths, etc
Difficult to get QABB to oviposit in the cages and breeding has not been possible

Propagation of vines
Techniques for raising food plant cuttings have been developed
3 months after planting of cuttings the vines are ready to plant out in the field
Even with best nursery techniques and use of hormone rooting gel, only about 2/3 of cuttings will
strike and grow through to planting
Further mortality occurs after planting out, so that only 50% of cuttings will develop into mature
vines
Been postulated that enrichment planting with food plant vines should increase the attractiveness
of an area for QABB, and boost its carrying capacity
Has been done by several landowners with good results
Community school butterfly gardens have also been developed at (1) Afore, (2) Aguido, (3)
Koruwo, (4) Gewoia, (5) Dea, (6) Umboworo, (7) Sakarina, (8) Bagou, (9) Ahora, (10) Ondahari

Background
In the light of Sime Darby Foundation’s generous grant to set up and staff for 3 years a
laboratory at Higaturu Estate, it was agreed desirable to check out the status of Queen
Alexandrae Birdwing (Ornithoptera alexandrae) (‘The Birdwing’) on the Plateau as well as the
status of the butterfly on the Higaturu Estate Lejo Forest Reserve. It was believed the Plateau
might be providing the remaining reserve for the last viable population of the butterfly.
I was accompanied on the visit by Charles Harbottle, an experienced entomologist who had
previously spent some time investigating the status of the butterfly in and around Higaturu
Estate.
The Managalas Plateau
The Plateau lies to the S.E. of Popondetta, and is accessed by a road turning off the road to the
sea, about 2 miles out of Popondetta. An excellent tarmac surface gives way after about 3
miles to a single track and at times deeply rutted route, initially over low coastal hills covered
with a native Acacia, and open lallang beneath – apparently fire climax vegetation. The road
then rises to the plateau – about 600 – 700 m above sea level. The road was originally
constructed around 1976 and for some years supported a bus service. The poor and
deteriorating condition of the road makes this no longer feasible and the road is only open in
dry weather to 4 w-d jeeps. We turned off just before dusk to the hamlet of Dareki – 7A Ward
3 – one of the 18 such on the Plateau, extending to 360,000 ha. Of this 80,475 ha is conserved.
The formalization of the conservation area is to be celebrated in the next couple of months.
The threats from mineral exploitation of the area (silver, nickel etc.) are thus reduced.
As a result of appalling roads the population of the Plateau, which has risen in recent years to
about 22,000 persons is poorly served: health and education facilities are minimal, there is no
power, and subsistence agriculture is the norm: bananas, taro, coffee and a little cocoa, the latter
greatly reduced by the activities of the cocoa pod borer. If roads were to be improved, there
are likely to be markets on the coast for agriculture products. This of course would put further
pressure on the remaining forest areas where the Birdwing occurs.
NGO Involvement
1

 There are a number of NGOs claiming involvement in the area.
1. Partners with Melanesians. Kenn Mondiai who kindly accompanied us on our visit is
one of the leading figures in this NGO. Kenn is extremely knowledgeable, way beyond
his formal training as a forester. He has been involved, after a stint at the University of
Papua, since 1989. This is a national NGO, registered on 8.8.98. All members of its
Board are PNG citizens. The NGO is entirely dependent on donor funding. They have
partnered with the Rainforest Foundation of Norway since 1996. They strongly
support the birdwing conservation programme. (But see his response to our press
release, attached as an Appendix.)
2. The Managalas Conservation Foundation (MCF). This is an umbrella organisaton for
all community based organizations on the Plateau.
3. Dadakul (Butterfly) a local organization works with MCF.
As far as we could gather, these organizations rub along together. It will be important for SDF
to be aware of, but not get involved in the politics of these organizations.
There was some dissatisfaction with Ausaid’s performance. When they left, they divided their
assets between different local organisations and nobody really benefitted. The operation run by
Cornwell Nukara and his brother Solomon Kotumba Bogina is a private initiative which
survived the pull out of Ausaid.
Existing Birdwing Breeding Operations on the Managalas Plateau.
The only existing Birdwing breeding operation on the Plateau is that of Cornwell Nukara and
his elder brother mentioned above. It operates about 40 minutes’ walk from Dareki village –
the walk involves wading through a couple of rivers and on through slightly overgrown
vegetable gardens, and leads to a small hamlet of 2 or 3 houses on the edge of the forest. Inside
the forest, much of the undergrowth has been cleared, except for saplings bearing Aristochia
dielsiana creepers. Many of these carried larvae or pupae of O. alexandrae or O. priamus. The
larvae appear to feed by preference on vines about 2-6 m above the ground.
When Cornwell and his colleagues find 6th instar larvae only, they transfer them on a length of
cut foodplant to the ‘greenhouse’ a wooden framed building about 4 m x 17m, 2.5 m high, 3 m
at the apex, Here the larvae are able to pupate in a protected environment, and emerge after 8
weeks as pupa (6 weeks on the plains) to extend and dry their wings before they are released
back into the forest.
In answer to our query, the brothers indicated that although they located and monitored all
smaller larvae within a radius of about 2 miles, they only collected the final instar larvae. They
said they could not afford to collect the younger larvae in view of the work involved.
When we asked to see some of the younger larvae which were not being harvested till the 6th
instar, we were met with excuses and prevarication – difficult to get through the forest etc. We,
naturally, saw no sign of any commercial business in the insect. However I was informed in
2

 Port Moresby that it is most unusual for PNG smallholders to maintain a project, apparently
unremunerated, for so long. Normally dead specimens are smuggled out across the Indonesian
border into W. Papua, and from there to Singapore, where they are imported as Indonesian
material. From there they are retailed on the black market to collectors in the developed world.
We should be more aware of, and keep our eyes open, to this possibility. We should bear in
mind that initially at least we may be dependent on the goodwill of Cornwell & family to obtain
breeding stock of O. alexandrae to get the laboratory started, and they may not be best pleased
if as a result of our breeding operations, the black market price drops – and with it the pressure
on wild populations. At the same time we do not wish to be associated with any aspect of the
black market operations. It is a matter which may well require some careful thought.
On the basis that each week they are rearing 1 or 2 O. alexandrae, this suggests, that with no
seasonality, as reported, they are breeding about 100 specimens a year: a significant
contribution to the population with a radius of about 2 miles. It is not clear what levels of
population exist elsewhere on the Plateau, but they may be not dissimilar.
We considered how best this population could be monitored, and concluded that
probably a tally of the numbers hatched each week would be the most reliable census.
The balance between
&
was reported to be close to 50 : 50, and
disappearance/loss of O. alexandrae on the vines was confined to the early instars.

♂ ♀

Status of O. alexandrae at Higaturu Estate.
About 3 years ago Charles Harbottle spent some time based at Higaturu Estate, with a view to
establishing the status of O. alexandrae at and around Higaturu Estate. In particular he had
retained records of the precise locations where 3 larvae had been found in 2014 on
Aristolochia vines on the estate’s Lejo Forest Reserve – a reserve of just under 50 ha. We
revisited the site and were delighted to discover that on precisely the same spot there was one
half grown O. alexandrae larva, which had been discovered about 3 days before our visit.
Other larvae and a pupa (suspected male) have since been found at the same spot. So we can
confirm that there is still a small residual population on the estate.
Unfortunately the reserve has been subject to much human disturbance, particularly near the
Aristolochia vines.
However in a way more interesting was the foodplant it was on. This was an Aristolochia vine
completely different from the one on which we had observed 6th instar larvae feeding on the
Managalas Plateau. Proof of this was the photograph taken 2 days before by the estate assistant
manager, Kenneth. This shows a fully opened flower, significantly different from the flowers of
what we assume was A. dielsiana on the Managalas Plateau. The flower had fallen and
disappeared by the time we arrived at the site, but we have asked Kenneth to forward the
photograph.
This may provide a clue to the riddle of the foodplant, where it has been reported that some
plants can provide food for the larva, while others prove toxic. It is just possible that there are
2 discrete populations, one feeding on the previously unknown vine in and around Higaturu and
another feeding on A. dielsiana on the Mangalas Plateau. Whether these are subspecies, or
conceivably a completely separate ‘crypto’ species, only DNA analysis will reveal. But is is
3

 certainly a very exciting prospect.
We believe that there may also be one or two remaining smallholder areas around Higaturu
with similar relict populations of the lowland form of the species.
At all events it will be important to collect cuttings from the vine at the Lejo FR, mark them
separately and grow them on in the Higaturu nursery.
The Proposed Lab & Nursery at Higaturu.
While on the estate we were shown the proposed site for the entomologist’s house, in the
housing compound, and also the secure area adjacent to Sangara Mill where it is proposed to
build the laboratory and housing for the guards. For security purposes we felt the guards’
houses should be completely fenced off from the lab. We also thought it might be best to move
the lab a few feet closer to the back fence so that it could benefit from afternoon shade provided
by the adjacent mature palms.
At the nursery we were shown cuttings of A. dielsiana sent down by Cornwell from Managalas.
There were approx. 200 of these, planted in polybags under shade. A number of them have
already begun to shoot. It was suggested that in future the corky stem be nicked with a penknife
to assist rooting and the stem laid horizontally and covered with +/- 2 cms of moist friable
topsoil.
Back in Port Moresby, Ian Orrell pointed out that for ‘speed cuttings’ it may be best to tie 5 or
6 polybags together, and as soon as the shoot from the central bag is long enough, peg it down
in an adjacent bag to develop its own roots This has been done successfully at WNB and we
should probably adopt it at Higaturu.
There are already a few A. tagala vines in polybags at Higaturu, and it would be a good idea to
let Cornwell and his colleagues have 2 or 3 of these to plant on his own land (where the plant is
rare or non-existent: see next section.)
In future individual vines from which cuttings are taken both at Managalas and Lejo should be
numbered and marked, the relevant cuttings likewise so that we can trace each plant back to the
parent.
The best way of growing the vines, once they have struck root, is probably to let them grow
over a trellis of rosewood as is being done in the nursery-making sure that neither the rosewood
nor the vines grow higher than 6’ to ensure ease of harvesting the leaves. Rosewood apparently
grows well from cuttings.
The aim should be to have adequate A. dielsiana vines, both in the compound round the
laboratory, with a plentiful back-up supply in the nursery in case of sabotage.
Next Steps
The SDF brief requires us to interact with and encourage smallholders to become involved in
breeding work. It is clear, subject to the reservations expressed above, that the prime
4

 candidates are Cornwell & his family. Probably the best approach would be:
(i)

To supply him with some polybag seedlings of A. tagala. This is the foodplant
of O. goliath, another very colorful species recorded on Managalas Plateau.
However A. tagala only occurs rarely there – and Cornwell’s plot apparently does
not have specimens. If wild O. goliath could be encouraged in Cornwell’s plot, he
would be in the remarkable position of being able to show eco-tourists 3
Ornithoptera species, which should be very beneficial for him.

(ii)

His ‘brother’/cousin Solomon Kotumba Bogina has attended ½ an agricultural
course at one of the PNG colleges, and was obliged to leave due to lack of funds. It
might be a good idea to finance him to do the remainder of his course (1 – 1.5
years?)

(iii)

At a later stage, if all goes well, we might consider, as has been done at the Dareki
village, providing materials for a basic rest house/hostel at Cornwell’s plot of land.
That at Dareki has 5 small unfurnished rooms and kitchen at one end. Probably a 2
room hostel would be adequate on Cornwell’s land – and would avoid the need for
visitors to trek up to the site, 40 minutes in the early morning to see the adults flying
– mostly 7.30 – 9.30 a.m.

We also considered the possibility of trying actively to encourage the development of ecotourism on the plateau – initially based at Dareki, but decided against it for the following
reasons:
(a) Severe access problems given the present state of the road.
(b) None of us have eco-tourism experience.
(c) There is a risk of unscrupulous black market dealers coming in.
It seems best if any genuine enthusiasts want to visit that they should make arrangements with
Partners with Melanesians, who through Kenn Mondiai appear to be well liked in the area.
On the NBPOL front, matters appear to be in order on the ground, with a team from SDF
visiting in early October to satisfy themselves on the financing and payment arrangements.
At a higher level the Governor of Oro Province, Gary Juffa, has expressed concerns, which
have now been allayed by making him in his capacity as Governor Patron of the project.
Acknowledgements.
Charles Harbottle and I would like to thank most warmly David Mather, his staff and Vijou
Vergis and his staff at Higaturu Estate. His staff accompanied us for 3 nights at Managalas, and
did everything possible to make us comfortable under the somewhat spartan conditions of PNG
village life. We are most grateful to them all.

5

 26 September 2017

6

national conservation and community development NGO working on the
Managalas plateau in Oro Province, I am not happy with this press statement and
it does not reflect on the work of PWM and our donor the Rainforest Foundation
of Norway in Oro for the past 33 years
and the work we are doing with the local CBOs and the Umbrella
Organisation for the people of Managalas plateau to protect the QABB.
This new project looks like a one sided work to promote the NBPOL,
Sime Darby Foundation just to fulfil your CSR Obligations, where the
efforts of PwM and the local people is not at all acknowledged and what
is there for the local people and there is no MOU to bridge the work
between PWM, MCF and the local people …all is just talks and I don’t
welcome this Press Statement. STOP and fix the issues like an MOU
before it goes out.
If this Press Statement Goes out as it is “We will not allow this project to
